description:
Hi! I’m Olesya, 16. I love astronomy, history, literature, geography, music, drawing, chess, and entomology. I study English and other languages, do archery, write scripts and character concepts.

For NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, I made a solo project that explains space through visuals, not complex formulas—so it won’t give you a headache. It’s for youth and general audiences. I did research, texts, visuals, and organization myself, and I’m ready to keep developing it independently.
summary: Cosmic Hourglass is an educational concept that makes complex astrophysics accessible to a broad, non-specialist audience. Using a simple everyday model—a folded sheet of paper and an hourglass—it visually demonstrates how the Einstein–Rosen bridge theory works in practice. Instead of relying on intimidating equations, the model clearly shows how space-time bends, how black holes pull in and stretch matter (spaghettification), and how white holes might eject that energy on the other side of space. This approach helps anyone easily understand fundamental cosmic processes and the possible cycle of the Universe.
details:
Complex astrophysical theories often remain locked behind advanced mathematics, making them inaccessible to the general public. Cosmic Hourglass bridges this gap by showing how the Einstein–Rosen bridge (a theoretical connection between black holes and white holes) works through a clear, tangible model that anyone—even a young child—can grasp.

How It Works (The Model): • Folded Space-Time: Take a standard A4 sheet of paper and bend it into an arch so the top and bottom halves face each other. This represents curved space-time connecting two separate regions of the Universe. • The Bridge: Place an hourglass between the two halves of the paper so its ends touch both surfaces. This hourglass acts as the tunnel linking the two spaces. • The Black Hole and Spaghettification: The opening on the top side of the paper is a black hole. It pulls in matter and light. As material is forced toward the narrow neck of the hourglass, extreme gravity stretches and crushes it—a real physical process called spaghettification. • The White Hole: Once compressed through the narrow neck, that energy and mass enter the bottom bulb of the hourglass. Where it meets the lower side of the paper, a white hole is formed. Unlike a black hole, a white hole prevents anything from entering and instead ejects all absorbed energy and matter outward. Because it opens on the "opposite side" of space-time, we cannot directly observe it from our side. • The Cosmic Cycle: The matter ejected by the white hole may accumulate to trigger a future Big Bang in another region of space. Meanwhile, on our side, black holes continue absorbing matter and merging with each other, eventually uniting all mass back into a single point.

Creativity, Tools, and Expected Impact: • Creativity & Factors Considered: Instead of relying on intimidating formulas or specialized jargon, our approach focuses on cognitive accessibility—translating abstract relativistic physics into everyday objects (paper and an hourglass) that a three-year-old can visualize. • Benefits & Impact: By turning complex theory into an intuitive visual mechanism, this project helps communicate big, important scientific ideas to a broad, non-specialist audience, sparking curiosity and making deep-space cosmology understandable to everyone. • Tools Used: Conceptual physics modeling, educational storytelling, and Google Slides for visual presentation.
